Module 0 — From question to meta-analysis

Start with the claim you want the evidence to support

Matthew Grainger

Learning objectives

By the end of this module, you should be able to:

  • explain what a meta-analysis does — and does not do;
  • translate an agri-food question into a clear estimand;
  • distinguish the target question from the available data;
  • identify when studies are sufficiently compatible to combine;
  • recognise why model choice comes after defining the question.

Open by asking participants what they hope a meta-analysis gives them. Common answers are “an overall effect”, “more power”, or “a definitive answer”. Keep these answers visible if possible. Return to them at the end.

The central message of the module is that meta-analysis is not primarily a software procedure. It is a way of estimating a clearly defined quantity from multiple studies.

What is meta-analysis?

Meta-analysis is the statistical synthesis of results from multiple studies addressing a sufficiently similar question.

It can help us estimate:

  • the average effect;
  • uncertainty around that average;
  • variation in effects among contexts;
  • whether observed differences can be explained by study characteristics.

Emphasise “sufficiently similar question”. Statistical compatibility does not establish conceptual compatibility. We can always put numbers into a model; that does not mean the resulting pooled estimate answers a useful question.

Interpretation

This is an important distinction for people who have encountered meta-analysis as a statistics exercise. A sophisticated model cannot repair biased eligibility criteria, selective evidence, poor extraction, or incompatible outcomes.

Mention that critical appraisal should inform interpretation and, where appropriate, sensitivity analysis; it is not simply a box to tick.

Start with the decision or claim

Suppose a policy colleague asks:

Does reduced tillage increase soil organic carbon?

Before opening R, ask:

  1. Compared with what?
  2. In which systems?
  3. Over what time period?
  4. Which measure of soil carbon?
  5. What kind of effect would answer the question?

Give participants 60–90 seconds in pairs. Ask them to identify what is underspecified. The aim is to show that apparently simple questions hide multiple analytical choices.

The question contains an estimand

An estimand is the quantity we want to estimate.

For our running example:

The average proportional difference in soil organic carbon under reduced tillage compared with conventional tillage, across eligible field studies and relevant agri-food contexts.

We still need to define:

Population/context · Intervention · Comparator · Outcome · Effect measure · Target quantity

Do not make this overly technical. “Estimand” is useful because it forces us to say exactly what number we want the synthesis to estimate.

Point out that the target quantity might be an average effect, a distribution of effects, an effect in a particular context, or something else. The pooled mean is not automatically the most decision-relevant target.

A useful translation exercise

Broad question

Does reduced tillage improve soil carbon?

More explicit synthesis question

Among agricultural field systems, what is the proportional difference in soil organic carbon under reduced or no tillage versus conventional tillage at the end of follow-up?

Effect measure

\[\ln(RR)=\ln\left(\frac{\bar X_{reduced}}{\bar X_{control}}\right)\]

Explain why the response ratio is attractive here: soil carbon is positive, studies may use different absolute scales, and a proportional effect has a meaningful interpretation. This is not a universal rule; Module 1 deals with choosing effect measures.

What evidence belongs together?

Two studies can both mention “soil carbon” and still estimate different things.

Consider differences in:

  • soil carbon measure and depth;
  • intervention definition;
  • comparator;
  • follow-up duration;
  • experimental design;
  • climate and soil system;
  • unit of analysis.

Pooling is a scientific judgement before it is a statistical operation.

Ask: “Would you combine soil organic carbon measured at 0–10 cm after one year with total carbon at 0–30 cm after 20 years?” There is no automatic yes/no answer. The point is that compatibility must be justified.

Variation is not necessarily noise

Agri-food interventions often operate differently across:

  • climates;
  • soils;
  • crops;
  • management histories;
  • intervention intensity;
  • duration.

A useful synthesis may therefore ask both:

What is the average effect?

and

How much do effects vary, and why?

Set up the later heterogeneity module. Avoid implying that heterogeneity is a statistical nuisance to be “fixed”. In applied ecology and agriculture it is often scientifically important.

The data do not define the question

A common workflow is:

“These are the outcomes reported in the papers. Which can we meta-analyse?”

A stronger workflow is:

“This is the quantity our question requires. Which reported results estimate it?”

That distinction helps prevent estimand drift.

Give an example: the management question concerns long-term soil carbon, but most studies report short-term microbial activity. Those data may be interesting, but pooling them does not answer the original question.

What does a pooled effect mean?

Imagine the synthesis eventually estimates a response ratio of 1.10.

That could be described as:

On average, soil organic carbon was approximately 10% higher under reduced tillage than under the comparator in the included evidence.

But this statement alone tells us nothing about:

  • how variable effects are;
  • whether the estimate is dominated by particular studies;
  • risk of bias;
  • applicability to a new setting.

Stress the phrase “in the included evidence”. Avoid jumping from a pooled estimate to a universal causal statement. The strength of causal interpretation depends on study designs and assumptions.

Before you meta-analyse: five questions

  1. What quantity do I want to estimate?
  2. Do the included effects estimate that quantity?
  3. Are the effects comparable enough to synthesise?
  4. Are observations statistically independent?
  5. What sources of bias or uncertainty affect interpretation?

These questions can become a recurring checklist throughout the course. Question 4 foreshadows the multilevel module. Question 5 links the statistical training back to evidence-synthesis practice.

Mini exercise: define the estimand

A review asks:

Do cover crops improve crop yield?

In pairs, specify:

  • population/context;
  • intervention;
  • comparator;
  • outcome;
  • effect measure;
  • target quantity.

Then ask: what decisions would change if the target were next-season yield versus mean yield over five years?

Allow about five minutes. There is deliberately no single perfect answer. Ask two groups to share their estimands and compare how small wording changes alter which studies/results would be eligible.

Take-home message

The question determines the estimand.
The estimand determines which effects are compatible.
Only then should the model be chosen.

Next: How do we put compatible study results onto an appropriate effect-size scale?

Return to the opening question: what does meta-analysis give us? Ideally participants now answer in terms of estimating a defined quantity and its uncertainty/distribution, rather than merely “combining studies”.
